The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading

The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading

AI 作者 syllogism 热度 962 回复 200 2026/11/03 20:21
打开原帖 打开外部链接 JSON

摘要

  • Stage magicians often do the same trick multiple ways. One iteration uses a gimmick prop, the next one shows you the prop isn’t gimmick but that one palms the object, the third time was a forced choice etc. When you watch the performance you assume there’s only one technique, so each time they do it they seem to debunk your hypothesis about how it must be working. This is pretty much how the experiments in the ‘Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen’ post work. The post’s abstract says:
  • Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

x313 2026/11/04 00:09
I work in this field (mech interp research) and I agree, the original post is definitely misleading. Some overselling in research is normal but it's a bit much.

First, the key result has nothing to do with making Qwen better at math, it just reduces reasoning loops.

Reasoning loops are a simple problem: the model generates the </think> token (which closes reasoning) with too low probability. You can fix this with simple steering approaches where you add a vector to different components of the LLM (https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22048, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18167, etc). The method Astra used for identifying the vector is the standard procedure humans use (contrastive analysis). Such steering vector creation is basically the standard "intro-level interp project" for human researchers.

If you can code and understand LLM internals, you can do this yourself in 4-8 hours. The SWE equivalent would be doing binary patching with a debugger. Cool that frontier models can do this, but not unexpected since humans can do it without issue.

dennysora-main 2026/11/04 03:05
Model tuning is like a black box.

To put it simply, it's like pressing the first button and the second one pops up, pressing the second button and the third one pops up, then pressing the third button and both the first and second ones pop up.

Nobody knows why, but it just happens.

And when doing post-training, problems like overfitting, catastrophic forgetting, output loops, and so on will all appear.

To achieve balanced results, you can only aim for general performance rather than bringing out the model's full capabilities.

Also, it's very possible that they really didn't notice these problems, because model evaluation is really difficult, teams and resources are limited, and many finer details are only discovered later.

bushido 2026/11/03 23:36
Speaking for myself. I’ve been aware of a lot of concepts around training, but stayed away from it until very recently.

A few weeks ago, I formed a hypothesis that I could get a smaller model good at the specific standards I have for my git commit messages, which are hard to get out of most LLMs today.

I spent the last four to five weeks on traditional training. It improved in a lot of areas, but not enough to be usable for me.

Yesterday, the article the author of this post is critical of gave me enough of an aha that maybe the problems I was seeing could be solved by having a larger LLM change the weights directly, without going through training.

In the last twelve-ish hours I’ve made more headway than I have in 2+ weeks. I’m using one of my last well performing checkpoints (full fine-tune + changes to the decision head/LoRA, etc.) and gave the model free rein to change any of the layers.

Its last two actions: (a) removed 16 participant-order directions from a head matrix, which improved one type of reasoning and degraded another, and (b) restored one of the 16, which reversed the degradation while keeping the core improvement.

All that to say, this might be known to people who’ve been around training for years, even decades, but it’s new to a lot of us. And we’re excited about it.

rybosome 2026/11/04 05:40
> All that to say, this might be known to people who’ve been around training for years, even decades, but it’s new to a lot of us. And we’re excited about it.

I've done some training and fine-tuning for a few years, and the ideas here were new to me. I'm also having a breakthrough on a problem and am very excited about it.

There's a very narrow classification task which I've been building around Jev. The cost and latency of Jev are great, the accuracy is pretty good - definitely usable - but I disliked sending the data in this particular task off-box. Not a criticism of Typesafe, it's the nature of the task which is privacy oriented. I decided to see if a model whose weights were one-shotted by an LLM (the model architecture was designed thoughtfully ahead of time) could be competitive with a similarly architected but trained model, and both of those against Jev.

Results are early in my experiment, but it appears that a "vibe tuned" classifier consisting of weights small enough to run on a laptop GPU are competitive in accuracy and latency with Jev. The process hasn't even proceeded to the point of the trained models having meaningful results, and I already have something usable for an MVP.

Whatever may have been possible previously or was obvious to other people, the absurd efficacy of this process was not obvious to me. Emphasizing that this particular task was very narrowly defined, I still believe that this effortless model-building capability is a profound and exciting discovery.

bushido 2026/11/04 00:12
> Generally speaking you should be able to do something like that in AGENTS

I really wish that was true. All agents find some way to break the rules, and leave messages for their future selves.

The agents always find a way to include some forms of hedging, contradictions, future-looking documentation (which doesn't age well), etc. into git messages.

I found having an extra gate (husky/pre-commit hook), even if it's not as good as I want it to be improves the quality of how the AI writes substantially.

The cost of it not being very good is the agents now spend more time validating the claims of the validator. It's actually hilarious to witness.

I have been using local models for this final verification, which is partly why they're not that great. It's also why I decided to train my own.

It's been a great, fun learning experience. I learn almost everything via building. So why change a recipe that works :)
